extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in mathematics or computer science learning to read and write proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing and presenting correct mathematical proofs, including proof structures, strategies for common logical forms, and how to use givens. Intended to teach students how to choose and organize proof methods based on the logical form of statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured proving / 'structured proving' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Many proofs are constructed by combining basic proof structures (e.g., suppose-until, for arbitrary x prove) and nesting them; choose proof structure guided by the logical form of the statement being proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of proofs like structured programs: combine basic structures, nest them, and use indenting in drafts to display structure. Although final write-ups are ordinary English paragraphs, you must understand underlying structure. Avoid using structural sentences (e.g., 'Let x be arbitrary', 'Suppose P') inappropriately (analogous to unmatched programming constructs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppose-until structure for implications
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement 'if P then Q', use the 'suppose-until' structure: suppose P is true and derive Q; then retract the supposition and conclude P → Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drafts you may indent the subproof; in prose introduce the assumption clearly and discharge it when Q is reached. Alternative: prove the contrapositive (see contrapositive rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: For-arbitrary-x structure for universal statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement of the form 'for all x, P(x)', declare x to be an arbitrary object and prove P(x); then retract the declaration and conclude the universal statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure x is truly arbitrary (not assumed special). If a letter is already used in the proof, choose a fresh variable. Do not misuse 'let x be arbitrary' as an isolated step without following through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write proofs in ordinary English paragraphs while preserving structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Although indented, structured forms help in planning, mathematicians usually write proofs in normal paragraphs; students should learn to translate structured drafts into clear paragraph proofs that reveal the underlying structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the structured draft to ensure correctness and then write fluent prose that conveys the same nested logical structure. Indenting is a drafting convenience; final presentation should read well but reflect the proof structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of valid argument
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument is valid if the premises cannot all be true without the conclusion being true as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge validity by logical form, not subject matter. Use substitution of propositional letters or truth tables to test validity; consider counterexamples where premises true and conclusion false to show invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of truth tables to analyze connectives and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use truth tables to determine how connectives (∧, ∨, ¬, →, ↔) affect truth values and to test logical equivalences and validity of argument forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct truth tables to analyze compound statements and to check tautologies or contradictions. Understand the truth-conditions for each connective (including conditional and biconditional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation goals (proving ¬P)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form ¬P: (a) reexpress as a positive statement; (b) use proof by contradiction (assume P and derive a contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reexpressing negatives can clarify the target. In contradiction proofs, identify which given you plan to contradict and aim to derive it. Proof Designer-specific PD notes suggest explicit commands, but the conceptual methods are reexpression and contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof of implication (P → Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P → Q directly: assume P and prove Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is typically the simplest approach for implications. Make the assumption explicit, derive Q, then discharge the assumption. Alternatively, use the contrapositive if more convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive for implications
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P → Q by contrapositive: prove ¬Q → ¬P instead (assume Q is false and prove that P must be false).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes proving the contrapositive is simpler than a direct proof. When given or able to prove ¬Q, use modus tollens to infer ¬P from P → Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction goals (proving P ∧ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a conjunction, treat it as two separate goals: prove P and prove Q separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can organize the proof so one conjunct follows from givens; if one conjunct is already given, only prove the other. Present both parts clearly so the conjunction is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunction goals (proving P ∨ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P ∨ Q: (a) assume ¬P and prove Q (or assume ¬Q and prove P); (b) use proof by cases, proving the disjunction in each exhaustive case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a strategy depending on available givens. Proof by cases splits the proof into exhaustive alternatives; when using the approach 'assume the other is false', make the assumption explicit and justify why that assumption is acceptable in the context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional goals (proving P ↔ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P ↔ Q, prove both P → Q and Q → P using methods appropriate for implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as two implications; you may reuse parts of proofs or structure to avoid repetition. State clearly that both directions have been proved to conclude the biconditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal quantifier goals (proving ∀x P(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove ∀x P(x) by letting x be an arbitrary object and proving P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the arbitrary choice is not restricted by hidden assumptions. Use a fresh variable if the proof context already binds x. After proving P(x) for an arbitrary x, conclude the universal statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential quantifier goals (proving ∃x P(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∃x P(x), find a value (a witness) of x that makes P(x) true, and prove P(x) for that value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either provide a concrete example or constructively define a witness and verify the property. If uncertain, you may introduce a variable as a placeholder but must later supply or justify the witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique-existence goals (proving ∃!x P(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: Two equivalent methods: (a) prove ∃x P(x) and prove uniqueness via ∀y∀z((P(y) ∧ P(z)) → y = z); (b) prove ∃x(P(x) ∧ ∀y(P(y) → y = x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either show existence and a separate uniqueness argument, or assert existence of a particular x and then prove any y satisfying P must equal x. Reexpress via definitions when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove statements ∀n ∈ N P(n) by induction: prove the base case P(0) and prove ∀n(P(n) → P(n+1)) (the induction step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the induction clearly: state base case, assume P(n) as induction hypothesis, and derive P(n+1). For some problems use strong induction: assume ∀k < n P(k) to prove P(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove ∀n[(∀k < n P(k)) → P(n)] — assume all smaller cases and deduce the case for n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when the n-th case depends on several smaller instances, not just n-1. State the stronger induction hypothesis explicitly and justify why the base cases cover the smallest required range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a given implication (P → Q) as an inference
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have P → Q and you also have P (or can prove P), then conclude Q (modus ponens). Conversely, if you have ¬Q, infer ¬P (modus tollens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you intend to use P → Q, either derive P or derive ¬Q depending on which direction helps. Make the application of Modus Ponens or Modus Tollens explicit in the chain of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling conjunctive givens (P ∧ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat a given conjunction as two separate givens P and Q (split it up and use each conjunct independently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly extract and name each conjunct you plan to use. This clarifies what facts are available for subsequent steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling disjunctive givens (P ∨ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proof by cases based on the disjunction; alternatively, if you can show one disjunct is false, conclude the other (disjunctive syllogism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using cases, make sure the cases are exhaustive. If you select the approach of proving one disjunct by showing the other false, justify why the negation holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal givens (∀x P(x)) use: universal instantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: From ∀x P(x) you may instantiate any particular value a and conclude P(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose what to substitute carefully; if you use a placeholder variable you must ensure it does not conflict with other bindings. Document the value plugged in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential givens (∃x P(x)) use: existential instantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: From ∃x P(x) introduce a new variable (a name for some object for which P holds) and reason with P of that new variable, taking care not to assume more about it than given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume properties of the witness beyond P. If you need a specific witness you may need to construct one or derive additional information from context.

rubrics_metrics.name: General proof techniques: proof by contradiction and proof by cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by contradiction: assume the negation of the goal and derive a contradiction. Proof by cases: divide possibilities into exhaustive cases and prove the goal in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are widely applicable techniques; for contradiction identify which given will be contradicted. For cases ensure coverage (exhaustive) and note whether cases are exclusive or may overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate English to logical form by meaning, not literal words
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating English statements into logical formulas, pay attention to meaning (e.g., 'and' in English sometimes expresses 'or'); determine logical form from semantics rather than word-by-word substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful reading is required: placement of 'either', 'both', 'but', 'either...or' can alter logical structure. Use symbols only after understanding the intended logical relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-formed formulas and parentheses conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Only certain combinations of connectives and statements form well-formed formulas; adopt conventions such as ¬ applying only to the immediately following statement and use parentheses to disambiguate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit parentheses only when conventions make expressions unambiguous. If needed, add parentheses to make main connective and grouping clear. Recognize meaningless strings and avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to disprove conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: A single counterexample suffices to show a conjecture is false; testing many examples may increase confidence but cannot prove a universal statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conjecturing patterns from examples, be cautious: only a proof establishes truth for all cases. Use counterexamples prominently to invalidate general claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose proof structure: match strategy to logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of proof structure is guided by the logical form of the statement (e.g., conditional suggests suppose-until; universal suggests 'let x be arbitrary'; existential suggests exhibit witness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the goal's form first; pick the canonical strategy for that form (summary of proof techniques provides a checklist). Combining forms may require nested structures. Plan the structure before detailed derivations.
